title: UCLA clobbers South Carolina for first NCAA national title in program history
content:
PHOENIX — With gold confetti falling from the rafters, Lauren Betts couldn’t hold back her tears.

As the final seconds of UCLA’s national championship game ticked off the clock, Betts and her teammates ran to midcourt and met in a massive hug. Players fell on the court, others jumped up and down, releasing both a sense of relief and jubilation.

The magical run by UCLA, which the Bruins began plotting after last season’s disappointing Final Four loss, ended in dominating fashion on Sunday when Betts and the Bruins defeated South Carolina 79-51. It capped the best season in the UCLA women’s basketball program’s history and gave coach Cori Close her first national championship.

It wasn’t a massive surprise that the Bruins were in this position. UCLA was the most talented team in the country and came into the NCAA Tournament as the second No. 1 seed. It has five players with the potential to be first-round picks in this month’s WNBA Draft. Still, South Carolina was the 3.5-point favorite coming into the championship.

That fact, and that everybody on the ESPN pregame panel picked South Carolina, left Betts dumbfounded. She couldn’t even find the words in the postgame news conference to express her feelings about being slighted. Her response was typical for the Bruins, who had locked in on their title goals all season, losing only once.

“I mean, I’m pretty sure people had us losing. You know what? I don’t even care,” Betts said. “We just won a championship, so you know what, I don’t really have much to say about that.”

Close, whose endearing in-game facial expressions and emotions circulate on social media often, said she was at ease before the game.

“I really did expect us to win today,” said Close, who is the first first-time champion head coach since Dawn Staley won her first title with South Carolina in 2017. “I thought about it several times. I’m like, we’re going to win. I felt very peaceful all day.”

For Staley, the loss marked her second straight championship game defeat. The Gamecocks lost 82-59 last year to UConn, and this year’s loss was even worse, the third-largest margin of defeat in women’s tournament history.

“Obviously, we got smacked today,” Staley said. “We’ve got to figure out how we smack back and put ourselves in the position where we’re hoisting the trophy at the end of the day.”

The Bruins dominated the title game from the opening tip, never relinquishing a lead or letting South Carolina breathe. UCLA was led by Gabriela Jaquez’s 21 points and 10 rebounds, while Betts had 14 points and 11 rebounds. All five starters scored in double figures as the Bruins shot 43 percent from the floor.

It was UCLA’s defense, and defensive game plan, that carried the Bruins to the championship, though.

The Bruins jumped out to a 14-3 lead five minutes into the game by baiting South Carolina’s post players into jump shots. South Carolina center Madina Okot made 1 of 5 shots in the first quarter, and the Gamecocks’ leading scorer, Joyce Edwards, missed all three attempts.

“I thought the first quarter, first half, we had a lot of people taking shots that aren’t normal for us,” Staley said. “So we didn’t do a good job of getting the people that probably was supposed to get some better looks the ball.”

That, mixed with UCLA’s guard pressure, kept South Carolina out of rhythm early, even when Betts went to the bench with two minutes left in the first quarter. Betts, UCLA’s 6-foot-7 All-America center, was struggling with her breathing on the bench and being treated by trainers.

She re-entered the game early in the second quarter, but the Gamecocks didn’t make a dent in the score with Betts on the bench. Instead, UCLA extended its lead to 12 points, going on a 10-4 run with its most impactful defender and post presence on the bench.

“I think our guards did a really good job of just taking away the point guard’s decision-making,” Betts said. “For me, my job is to just protect the rim. Whatever they told me to do today in the scout, whether it’s guard them out there, just protect the paint, I was going to do what I got to do.”

The Bruins crushed South Carolina from there. UCLA outscored the Gamecocks 58-41 in the final three quarters and never gave South Carolina any hope. The Gamecocks were led by 14 points from Tessa Johnson, while Agot Makeer chipped in 11 points off the bench.

For UCLA, this was a dream realized. The Bruins have been knocking on the door since they reached the Sweet 16 four years ago. Now, Close has not only won her first championship but has also established herself as one of the premier program builders in the country.

“It really is only meaningful because of the people I get to share it with,” Close said.

Last season, UCLA left the Final Four in tears after its 85-51 semifinal loss to UConn. On Sunday, it did again, but this time the tears came as they danced at mid-court, as champions, the first ones in program history and the first Big Ten champions since Purdue won in 1999.

“I do think that experience playing at the Final Four last year helped us just in our preparation from the spring to now,” Kiki Rice said. “We knew what to expect. We knew what it would take to win at that level. Having that experience, I feel like we were able to set our minds coming into this tournament, coming into the Final Four. This is what it’s going to take to win it.”
